insipid

in-SIP-id · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Insipid is boring, or lacking flavor or interest.

The soup was so insipid that the diners reached for the salt and pepper before taking a second bite.

Example

Critics panned the sequel as insipid, a flat retread of the original with none of its wit or surprise.

Insipid applies just as easily to food, writing, or personality -- anything that fails to leave any real impression.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bland: Bland means mild and gentle in flavor or character, and it is barely a criticism — bland food can be a deliberate, soothing choice for an upset stomach. Insipid is harsher: it condemns food, writing, or people as disappointingly dull and lifeless.

dull: Dull means not interesting or exciting, and it covers almost anything, from a gray sky to a slow afternoon. Insipid is more pointed: it says something promised flavor or spark and delivered nothing, leaving no impression at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

flavorful: having a strong, pleasant taste

zesty: full of lively flavor or energy

Where it sits · how empty of interest it is

plain → insipid → mind-numbing

plain vs. insipid: Plain is much milder than insipid: plain just means nothing added — a plain bagel, a plain white wall — while insipid condemns something that should have had flavor or spark and delivered none.

mind-numbing vs. insipid: Mind-numbing sits well above insipid: insipid writing merely fails to leave an impression, while a mind-numbing lecture is so crushingly dull it seems to switch your brain off.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root+suffix — sipid: tasty, flavorful (Latin (sapidus))

Put it together: in- ("not") + sipid ("tasty") = lacking flavor or interest.

Use the root in a new word: sapient: Dad packed a bag of savory snacks for the long train ride north.

Word Choice

Insipid works equally well for food that lacks flavor and for writing or people that lack any spark of interest.
